title.value: Our AI Midwife

hits.author: semiquaver
hits.title: Our AI Midwife

story_text.value:
I’ve been using AI agents to build systematic strategies on Hyperliquid for over a year, and slowly built up a reliable system to represent, test and deploy strategies. Typically there are a few options 1) llm in the execution loop, ie it makes decisions and trades, but that is slow, inconsistent and hard to audit 2) you have an agent write all the code, backtest etc, but it makes tons of subtle mistakes with time series data and diff timeframe etc, and is often not reusing bits. There are some ways to improve this of course with right frameworks and setups. But its still hard to be confident in its correctness and its hard for you to verify quickly.

With Keel we built a small typed language (DSL) to represent strategies. It uses a well defined set of components to build a DAG of steps, it carries types and clocks. This allows agents to build these strategies with a really fast feedback loop as they can be quickly validated and many common errors avoided. In a DAG its also easy to inspect intermediate results. Valid strategies are fingerprinted and the exact same artifact runs in backtesting and live. These strategies are also much easier for humans to verify as they are self describing components, and mostly linear to read and reason about.

Still trying to improve the space of how many types of different strategies can be represented in this and still trying to improve how well LLMs go from natural language to strategy. A lot of the improvements come from just giving the agents better and faster tools and faster feedback loops.

title.value: Show HN: Keel – Give your agent a typed strategy language, not a trading account

story_text.value:
Hey HN,

Some friends and I built an app called Sidekick that joins your telehealth visits in real-time. It explains medical terms and suggests useful questions, including ones you may not have thought to ask. After the visit, it provides a summary including next steps, so you can focus on the conversation instead of taking notes.

The idea of Sidekick came from our team's experiences with healthcare. Our founder, Rahul, had stage three cancer at 17. His mom had to manage everything around his care: taking notes through treatment, figuring out what questions to ask, etc. A decade later and he’s now in remission, but still sees a lot of specialists and deals with the same challenges.

Another teammate became a caregiver after his dad had a severe stroke. He found himself taking notes, looking up medical terms, and trying to keep track of what was said during every doctor visit. Others have dealt with situations like this when navigating pancreatitis and other serious health issues.

These experiences got us interested in how we might be able to reduce the burden on the patient or caregiver.

A lot of products focus on simply recording or summarizing the visit. That's useful and a step in the right direction, but we kept coming back to the fact that a lot of the challenge originates while the conversation is still happening. If you can catch something in the moment, you can address it with your clinician immediately and potentially lead to better outcomes. If you realize you missed something after the visit, then you have to try to get another appointment (and in SF I often can't get another doctor visit till 2 months later).

So we built Sidekick, to help patients and caregivers during a visit in real-time to translate medical jargon and suggest useful questions, ideally without becoming a distraction.

If you want to try it, you can download it on our website. Sidekick is desktop-only for now, but we’re working on a mobile app for in-person visits.

We would be especially interested to hear feedback on the live part of the experience. What are your thoughts on the balance between live help vs after-visit? Would something pre-visit be more helpful?

title.value: Show HN: We built a real-time desktop companion for patient's telehealth visits

story_text.value:
Hi HN! I've made it possible for you to make product roadmaps like you'd make an RPG skill tree, or a tech tree in a video game.

Ever since seeing WoW talent trees* in high school i've been obsessed with RPG skill trees as a way to represent information as I've thought they convey 1) Ordering, 2) Progression and 3) Contingent Requirements really well. Not only do they help give better visual structure of whats happening and what will happen - they also give people a feeling of movement, progression and hope (whereas kanban boards and issue trackers give people the feeling of dread).

This isn't surprising as video games were really designed to make people excited to play on and reach the next milestone.

Turns out this format is really fun for people and agents to think about their products! As an experiment I also hooked up an MCP to one of my product roadmaps and it was able to map out my current codebase to a kanmap, and then suggest realistic next ideas to make. I've even got an agent now working on the next node of a kanmap.

* Kanmaps was inspired not just by WOW talent trees, but also by the Age of Empires Tech Trees, and FFX ability spheres setup. Also huge shoutout to a bank in Australia called Up who did something called the Tree of Up as a product roadmap like a video game for their banking product - their work definitely inspired things in Kanmaps too.

title.value: Show HN: Kanmaps – Product roadmaps like videogame skill trees

story_text.value:
Dear fellow HNers: I said my account has a max karma of 32767, and I'm about to hit that limit. So, for my final post, I'd like to share some of my individual aspirations:

* Be honest. We shouldn't lie, manipulate, dark-pattern, etc. We should invest towards a society that can trust each other, and the first step is our own behavior.

* Be reliable. We should make things that work, follow through on promises, represent prospects in good faith, etc.

* Be helpful. We should help colleagues, random strangers, and society in general. Not maneuver to exploit them.

* Be smart. We're not as smart as we think we are, and we are often dumb. Especially when it comes to topics in which we actually have little experience. Also when we're overconfident about something we "know".

* Be humble. We can make mistakes about even the things we know best, and we should always be learning.

* Be constructive. Others make mistakes, too, and we should help them when they do, as we'd want them to help us or our friends&family, when we make mistakes.

* Be decent. No one person deserves a billion dollars of humanity's wealth. Few people agreed to the rules that enable that: it's not a game that we are winning; it's collusion against the masses, which some people hop onto. Also applies to some smaller sums.

* Be sane. If we find ourselves with way more money than our share, then we say, "oops, how embarrassing", and spread it back around, to everyone. We shouldn't be like the billionaire who instead decides all the poors or immigrants or feminists or trans people or artists or kindergarten teachers or whoever are somehow shortchanging billionaires.

* Be introspective. See sane, above.

That's it for now. See you around. I'll continue to be in the world and in tech industry, but it's time for me to take an HN break. If I come back, it might as well be a new account.

title.value: Tell HN: Thanks for All the Fish

story_text.value:
I made this for kids around 10 to 14. A robot called Errol solves a math problem step by step and one of the steps is wrong. The kid has to find it and say what's wrong with it. Sometimes nothing is wrong, so just saying "there's a mistake" every time doesn't work. The user needs to enter an explanation if she finds an error to gain more XP; speed matters also for more points. There is no direct interaction or chatting with an LLM. Lathoa's harness is stable and has many evaluation steps to catch inconsistencies and prompt injections.

You can play one on the homepage without signing up.

The part that surprised me: it's hard to get an LLM to be wrong on purpose. Half the time it gives you the right answer and calls it wrong, or a "mistake" that's actually correct. So every case gets checked before a kid sees it. Where it can, a plain arithmetic check redoes the math exactly. A second model also solves the problem without seeing Errol's work. If anything disagrees, the case is thrown away.

The weak spot is that the second model can make the same mistake as the first. The arithmetic check is there for that, but it only works on English cases so far. German and Greek write decimals with a comma and I haven't got the parsing right yet.

What I'd really like to know: does finding someone else's mistake teach anything that solving the problem yourself doesn't? I'm not sure, and I'd like to hear from people who teach.

title.value: Show HN: Lathoa, a math app for kids where the AI is wrong on purpose

story_text.value:
Hi folks!

Because of AI, there is more code to review. I don't know about you, but I get annoyed when the default git diff doesn't match something "obvious". I built CodeDiff to help.

It's a syntax-aware, careful implementation in Rust of all current research in code diffing. It parses 24 languages with TreeSitter and falls back to a modified Myers line diffing algorithm for any file it cannot parse. I wouldn't necessarily call it a novel algorithm, but it isn't a re-implementation of existing tools either.

I tested it on the last 50 commits of all 7400-or-so repositories that are in the Gentoo package list. CodeDiff can diff 99.95% of those file pairs in 120s and 6GB of RAM on a rusty 11 year old Intel E3-1275 v5. The median speed is 7ms and 93% of files are diffed in under 100ms.

I also did a bit of hand solving and have a test dataset of 1400 hand solved diffs. CodeDiff is perfect on 70% and near-perfect on 90% of them. But accuracy is actually a complex thing to measure, because if you are only after the AST diff, then it is perfect 89% of the time. Deciding what to paint however is not an objective thing so if you do try it out, check out the render options (press M) and make it fit your style.

If you just want to see how it looks like: https://ivankovic.github.io/codediff/showcase/?case=python-r...

If you want to install it: https://github.com/ivankovic/codediff

Do feel free to file issues. It's v0.1.1 at the moment, but I have been using it for months as my git difftool and I plan to keep that stable. Using it as a library directly from Rust however, might change until v1.0. The final goal for v1.0 is p99 < 400ms and 99% perfect diff, including multi-file diff support in 30 languages.

Credit where credit is due: There is a bunch of people researching diffs in the past 20 or so years. Without those papers, CodeDiff would be a lot harder to build. Especially without APTED and Myers algorithms.

License: AGPL3.0, I kind of like copy-left. If your company prevents use of AGPL software tell them to throw a few bucks my way for my token usage and we can talk.

AI disclosure: I use AI assisted coding. Claude and Mistral were used, heavily.

title.value: Show HN: CodeDiff – Fast (<100ms), robust (99.95%) syntax-aware code diff
